https://www.developingtelecoms.com/telec.text: Energy & Sustainability Smart city solutions aim to reduce Warsaw’s lighting expenditure Details Vaughan O'Grady Category: Energy & Sustainability 07 August 2026 6177 views Investment Central and Eastern Europe Poland Cloud Platform Smart Cities Lighting Emitel, which says it delivers digital services and solutions powered by infrastructure, technology and data, has won a contract to build an intelligent street lighting control system for Warsaw. The smart city solutions deployed will enable Warsaw to reduce electricity consumption and make more efficient use of its existing infrastructure. Municipal services will also be able to respond to faults more quickly and carry out maintenance work more effectively. The value of the core project is said to be close to PLN79 million (about US$21.2 million). This is a strategic investment designed to modernise over 110,000 luminaires, representing a substantial proportion of the city’s lighting infrastructure. The new system will enable remote lighting management, early fault detection and dynamic adjustment of light intensity. The agreement covers the development and maintenance of IT systems, a cloud-based infrastructure management platform, the supply of lighting controllers and the equipping of a dedicated management centre. The contract has been signed for eight years, with an option to extend it for a further five. As part of the project, Emitel will build bith the system and a modern Lighting Management Centre. Equipped with operator workstations and a video wall, the centre will provide real-time management and visibility of the city’s lighting infrastructure. Lukasz Puchalski, Director of the Municipal Roads Authority of the Capital City of Warsaw, explains that over the course of five years, it has replaced all lighting fixtures in Warsaw, saving approximately US$16.1 millon annually. About US$17.4 million has been investted in the replacement of these fixtures, and the savings achieved have already reached nearly US$40.2 million. He adds: “Ultimately, Warsaw’s street lighting will be able to operate using only about 20% of the electricity required just a few years ago. And we will continue to allocate the saved funds to further investments.” Using the controllers, the Lighting Management Centre will not only be able to monitor changes in luminaire performance in real time but also make adjustments remotely. Once the new system is operational, settings will be adjustable even on a daily basis, for example in response to weather conditions. This will ensure that street lighting is used precisely when residents need it. The system will also make it possible to optimise the output of each individual luminaire. On streets with highly reflective surfaces, such as light-coloured roadways, lamps will be able to operate at lower power. The city will also be able to reduce lighting levels on local streets where traffic is very light at certain times of night. Based on the adopted estimation model, Emital says annual energy savings could reach up to 30%. More Articles you may be Interested in... https://www.euronews.com/2026/09/08/turk.text: Kemal Kılıçdaroğlu returned as interim leader of Turkey's main opposition Republican People's Party (CHP) earlier this year after a court annulled the 2023 leadership election that had removed him — and he says jailed Istanbul Mayor Ekrem İmamoğlu is not a political prisoner, while leaving the door open to supporting an İmamoğlu presidential bid.In an exclusive interview with Euronews at CHP headquarters in Ankara, Kılıçdaroğlu defended his court-ordered return, acknowledged the party split would cost the CHP votes and called for Turkey to lead a new regional peace organisation.İmamoğlu was arrested in March 2025 on corruption charges, triggering Turkey's largest street protests in more than a decade.His supporters say the charges are politically motivated, noting his status as Erdoğan's most credible electoral rival.His 2019 victory ended 25 years of AKP and other rule in Istanbul and his re-election in 2024 reinforced that standing. The government has rejected accusations of political interference.Kılıçdaroğlu said İmamoğlu's potential candidacy for the presidency did not make the corruption case political."Being a presidential candidate is one thing. These cases are another," he said, noting that he had voted for İmamoğlu in the CHP's own presidential primary.But Kılıçdaroğlu said İmamoğlu should not have been detained while awaiting trial. "He can stand trial, but I did not think it was right to detain him. I still hold that view today."A separate legal complication arose when Istanbul University annulled İmamoğlu's degree in March 2025, raising questions about his presidential eligibility — Turkey's constitution requires candidates to have completed higher education.İmamoğlu has since joined Yeni Parti, the breakaway political group led by his ally Özgür Özel.Asked whether he would back an İmamoğlu presidential bid if those legal obstacles were resolved, Kılıçdaroğlu did not give an unconditional endorsement but said talks would be needed and stressed that opposition unity was a mathematical necessity."How will you get 51%? By working together. How can you get it without working together?" he said. "There is no place for grudges, anger or hostility in politics."The CHP was founded by Mustafa Kemal Atatürk in 1923 as the party of the Turkish republic and its founding secular ideology, known as Kemalism.It governed Turkey without interruption until 1950 and remains the main vehicle for secular, centre-left politics. It draws its core support from western Turkey's urban and coastal populations, civil servants, professionals and voters who prioritise secularism and EU integration.A court-ordered returnKılıçdaroğlu, who led the CHP for 13 years, came closer to defeating Erdoğan than any opposition candidate in two decades when he ran against him in the May 2023 presidential election.The race went to a second round — the first runoff in Turkish history — where Erdoğan won 52.2% to Kılıçdaroğlu's 47.8%.The result ended the most serious electoral challenge to Erdoğan's rule and directly triggered the CHP leadership contest that replaced Kılıçdaroğlu with Özel. İmamoğlu backed Özel in the party contest.A court ruling on 21 May annulled that congress and restored the previous leadership on an interim basis. Özel's leadership team denied the vote-buying allegations and accused the government of using the judiciary against the party.Özel has appealed the ruling, leaving Kılıçdaroğlu's interim leadership subject to further judicial review.Kılıçdaroğlu denied any involvement in the case. "I am not a party to this case. I did not file it. I did not testify. I have no involvement in this case," he said.Asked whether returning through a court ruling rather than a delegate vote bothered him, he said the ruling had restored the full previous leadership, not just him personally.Asked whether accepting the ruling implied trust in the judiciary, he replied: "Who said I trust the judiciary?"The cost of CHP's splitThe CHP came first in Turkey's 2024 local elections under Özel, retaining Istanbul and Ankara and dealing a major setback to Erdoğan's ruling AKP.Turkey's parliament has 600 seats. With 91 MPs, Yeni Parti is now the second-largest parliamentary group after the ruling AKP and the largest opposition bloc, while the CHP has 44 MPs.Kılıçdaroğlu insisted that his party's core voters remained loyal, but acknowledged that the division would come at a cost."Will it lose strength? Of course it will. But we will recover over time. No one should be concerned," he said.Citing his own unsuccessful presidential bid in 2023, he argued that political success could no longer be measured solely by parliamentary seat totals."A party's success now depends on its presidential candidate winning," he said.He also said he had instructed provincial party leaders not to criticise or quarrel with Yeni Parti, and remained willing to meet Özel."It is the government we should be criticising," he said.Erdoğan's current presidential term runs until 2028. Whether he is constitutionally eligible to stand again is disputed: Turkey's constitution limits presidents to two terms, but the AKP argues the clock reset when the new presidential system took effect in 2018, making 2028 effectively his first term under the new rules.The Constitutional Court has not definitively ruled on the question. If he does stand, he would face an opposition that is currently divided.Turkey 'a leading force for peace'Asked about Turkey's role in the conflict between Israel and Iran, Kılıçdaroğlu called for closer cooperation among regional countries."Turkey should not want war in its region. It should be a leading force for peace," he said.He pointed to the CHP's proposal for a Middle East Peace and Cooperation Organisation, initially led by Turkey, Iran, Iraq and Syria, which he said could later expand.Regional countries should work together to secure peace, economic integration and stability, he argued.Relations between Turkey and Israel deteriorated over the Israel-Hamas war in Gaza, with Ankara suspending bilateral trade in May 2024. Their rivalry also extended into Syria after Bashar al-Assad's fall.Kılıçdaroğlu also condemned what he described as Israel's threatening stance towards Turkey."It is absolutely unacceptable for Israel to threaten Turkey," he said. "Israel does not even have the right to criticise Turkey."

https://wowo.com/community-arts-program-.text: Home Local News Community Arts Program to host fifth annual Java, Jive & Pie fundraiser WINONA LAKE, Ind. (WOWO) — The Community Arts Program of Kosciusko County will bring the sounds of the 1940s to Winona Lake next month for its fifth annual Java, Jive & Pie fundraiser and gala. The event, themed “The Village Canteen,” will be held Saturday, Oct. 24, at Rodeheaver Auditorium, 901 Park Ave. A dance lesson begins at 6 p.m., followed by the musical program at 7 p.m. This year’s event will feature music inspired by the 1940s swing era and USO shows. Matt and Cindy Smith of Art of Dance Warsaw will provide dance instruction before the program, and guests are encouraged to dress in period attire and take part on the dance floor. The Vocal Vibes adult vocal jazz ensemble will perform songs from the era, while Wally Brath and The Village Canteen Band will provide instrumental music. The evening will also include charcuterie, coffee, pie, a silent auction and a live auction. Proceeds from the fundraiser support the Community Arts Program and its mission to provide creative and collaborative opportunities for people in Kosciusko County to develop and share their musical and artistic talents. Tickets are $40 per person or $300 for a table of eight. Corporate sponsorships and donations are also available. https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026.text: Mary Peltola launches her Senate campaign in Anchorage, Alaska, on 17 January 2026. Photograph: Kerry Tasker/Reuters View image in fullscreen Mary Peltola launches her Senate campaign in Anchorage, Alaska, on 17 January 2026. Photograph: Kerry Tasker/Reuters US midterm elections 2026 Trump’s war and tariffs have battered Alaska. A pro-oil Democrat could flip the key Senate seat Democrats believe circumstances have aligned for them to win a slew of competitive elections in the state Chris Stein in Anchorage, Alaska Thu 22 Oct 2026 06.00 EDT Last modified on Thu 22 Oct 2026 06.01 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google M ary Peltola’s campaign to represent Alaska in the US Senate has taken her to parts of the massive state’s interior that are inaccessible by road and on the frontlines of the cost-of-living crisis she hopes will make her the first Democrat to win the seat in nearly two decades. She has been to towns where paper towels retail for $40, a half gallon of oat milk goes for $21 and the cost of a new freezer can be quadruple what it is in the state’s largest city, Anchorage, simply because it’s so complicated to get there. Along the Arctic Ocean, she’s heard of communities where power bills have climbed to $1,500 a month because they rely on generators for power and the Iran war has pushed the cost of diesel to new heights . “Nobody can afford that,” Peltola said in an interview. Alaska, a right-leaning state that’s about twice the size of Texas but the third least-populous in the country, has always been among the more expensive places to live, and the price increases in the state’s rural areas haven’t necessarily been felt to the same degree in the more populous cities and towns. Yet the state’s Democrats believe circumstances have aligned for them to win a slew of competitive elections in the 3 November midterms. The Senate seat currently held by two-term Republican Dan Sullivan is a top prize. “In 23 short days, we’re going to be voting both [Republican congressman] Nick Begich and Dan Sullivan out of office, and they richly deserve it,” the chair of the state Democratic party, Eric Croft, said at a press conference last week. “They are self-serving, self-dealing DC politicians who repeatedly voted to make life harder and more expensive for Alaskans.” View image in fullscreen The Republican US senator Dan Sullivan after a debate with Mary Peltola in Anchorage, Alaska, on 15 October 2026. Photograph: Kerry Tasker/Reuters All signs indicate that Republicans are taking seriously the threat posed by Peltola, an Alaska native and former US House lawmaker who supports oil and gas and gun rights. Outside groups have poured in tens of millions of dollars into supporting both candidates, and last week Donald Trump made the long journey from Washington DC to the conservative Matanuska-Susitna valley to rally voters behind Sullivan, who has trailed in some recent polls . “Here in Alaska, the Democrats are running radical left Mary Peltola for the Senate. If she gets in, you’re screwed,” the president told a packed sports center in Wasilla, which is best known outside the state as being the home town of Sarah Palin , the Republican former vice-presidential nominee. Getaway cars, affairs, Dubai fugitives: Trump’s pick Ken Paxton brings baggage to Senate race in Texas Read more On the campaign trail, Peltola and Sullivan have dueled over who would do a better job lowering costs for Alaskans, and also representing its vital fishing and oil and gas industries in the US Capitol. There have been mutual accusations of allegiances not to a state known as “the last frontier” but to special interests in the Lower 48, while Sullivan has accused Peltola of denigrating Alaskans after a report that she mistreated her staffers. The incumbent has his own unique vulnerability in the form of a similarly named Republican challenger who made it through the state’s top-four primary, and could split his support. And while polls open on 3 November, the outcome may not be known for days – Alaska has always taken a long time to count its ballots, and its use of ranked-choice voting in the Senate contest could result in an even lengthier wait for the final result. No state like it Since becoming the 49th state in 1959, Alaska has only once supported a Democratic candidate in a presidential election – Lyndon B Johnson in 1964. But its politics are nuanced – bipartisan majorities currently control the legislature and the frontrunner in the governor’s race is a Democrat . In the race for the state’s lone US House seat, the party has coalesced behind the independent candidate Bill Hill to take on Begich. “Sixty per cent of Alaskans do not identify with the Republican or the Democratic party. We are a great example in this state of how government should work,” Hill, who is receiving support from the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, said in an interview. A former state lawmaker, Peltola rose to prominence in 2022 when she won a special election to replace Don Young, the long-serving Republican congressman who died at 88 , and became the first Alaska native in Congress. She was elected to a full term later that year, then lost re-election to Begich in 2024. This year, Peltola is viewed as the best candidate Democrats could field to take on Sullivan. View image in fullscreen A fish hatchery in Valdez, Alaska, on 23 August 2023. Peltola centers her campaign on the slogan “fish, family, freedom”. Photograph: Michael Siluk/Universal Images Group/Getty Images Centering her campaign on the slogan “fish, family, freedom”, she has added an Alaskan twist to the cost-focused platform many Democrats have adopted nationwide. Visitors to her campaign website can play a video game intended to highlight her views on bycatch, or the accidental netting of other species by trawlers, which has become a major controversy in Alaska as salmon runs have dwindled. Peltola opposes Trump’s tariff regime, noting it has driven up costs for imports from Canada, which separates Alaska from the rest of the country. She has also condemned his decision to attack Iran and spark a conflict that has driven costs for gasoline and diesel – which typically arrive by barge or ship in the state’s interior and island communities – even higher than usual. “These really frivolous decisions are just putting Alaskans in a bind, and we’re really paying the price for these weird partisan wars,” Peltola said as she visited a picket line of flight attendants at Anchorage’s main airport. With a laugh, she added: “I don’t know what’s funny about that, but it’s funny.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly, plus breaking news alerts Sign up to The Stakes 2026 A weekly guide to what really matters in the US midterms, plus breaking news alerts. after newsletter promotion Sullivan, her opponent, was first elected in 2014 after ousting a Democratic incumbent. He serves alongside Republican Lisa Murkowski, Alaska’s senior senator who is one of the most outspoken Trump critics in the Senate, but has nonetheless remained a firm ally of of the president, even as his popularity has waned , unlike many vulnerable Republicans who have sought distance. Sullivan has emphasized his advocacy for Alaska’s military installations, as well as the state’s long list of proposed oil developments and major infrastructure projects that he argues will only come to fruition if Republicans are kept in charge. View image in fullscreen Demonstrators march during the No Kings protest in downtown Anchorage on 28 March 2026. Photograph: Hasan Akbas/Anadolu/Getty Images “Joe Biden, Schumer, their Democratic allies came after Alaska with a barrage of executive orders to shut down our state, kill jobs, drive up the cost of energy, and my opponent, Mary Peltola, not only did nothing to stop it, she enabled it,” Sullivan said as he rallied with Trump. “They try to kill our jobs and turn us into a national park. Ladies and gentlemen, the conflict in the Middle East is temporary. The true forever war is the national Democrats’ war against Alaska oil and gas and our jobs.” He gained new ammunition against Peltola in September, when the New York Times reported allegations that she had verbally and physically abused her staff and used slurs. “My opponent really doesn’t like her fellow Alaskans. She just doesn’t,” Sullivan told supporters in Wasilla. Peltola’s campaign has said parts of the report are not true, and noted some of the behavior occurred when she was grieving the death of her husband in a plane crash, and the death of her mother around the same time. When Peltola was asked about the report during a debate with Sullivan last week, she replied: “I do not think that this election is about me on my worst day, and I found so many of these allegations concerning and outright fabrications.” ‘Priced out of petroleum’ Alaska is one of the nation’s top oil-producing states, and every year its permanent fund pays each resident a dividend that’s usually upwards of $1,000 . But production, which is concentrated on the state’s North Slope, has steadily declined since peaking in the late 1980s, and how to manage the resource is a constant topic in the state’s politics. View image in fullscreen A caribou on the tundra near the Trans Alaska pipeline system on 9 May 2025 near the Atigun pass in Alaska. Photograph: Lance King/Getty Images Sullivan is all-in on oil production, supporting moves by Trump to open up more protected federal land and waters to drilling, which could offer new revenue opportunities. He cheered the president’s announcement that South Korea would invest $54bn to build a long-discussed natural gas pipeline across the state, although reports have since emerged that Seoul has agreed to no such deal. Though she was in the House of Representatives for just over two years, Peltola has taken credit for pushing Joe Biden to approve the massive Willow oil project , over the objections of environmentalists. But she also emphasizes the opportunities renewable energy could present to Alaska’s communities, and is cognizant that she is a member of a party that prioritizes fighting the climate crisis, which many believe requires curbing oil and gas production. “We do need more oil production in our state for our state revenues to pay for our schools, our roads, our public safety,” Peltola said. But the sky-high prices for gas in parts of Alaska are proof to the candidate that oil is not the solution alone. “When you’re paying $26 a gallon for gas or diesel, we’re priced out of petroleum,” she said. https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/10/28/eu-e.text: Menü Kereső Ránk számíthattok! 3000 új támogatót keresünk Csatlakozom Érezhető változásról, de hiányosságokról is beszélt a Budapesten vizsgálódó EP-küldöttség vezetője Külföld Márton Balázs Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom Érezhető változásról beszélt szerdán az Európai Parlament (EP) Magyarországra látogató küldöttségének elnöke. Sophie Wilmès hangsúlyozta: sokakkal találkoztak a háromnapos látogatásuk alatt, a kormányzat és a köztársasági elnök mellett többek között bírókkal, a civilekkel és ellenzéki pártok képviselőivel is. Hangsúlyozta, hogy amikor tavaly egy küldöttséggel Budapestre érkeztek, folyamatosan romlott a helyzet, az előző kormány ellenséges volt, és nem akart változtatni az irányon. Többek között veszélyhelyzeti rendeletekkel kormányzott, gyorsítva elfogadott jogszabályokkal, nyomás volt az igazságügyön, a kormány narratívája uralta a médiát, a független szervezetek ellenséges atmoszférában dolgoztak. A tavalyi látogatásukkor látták az európai politikusokat támadó állami plakátokat is. A kormányváltás óta megszűntek a civilek elleni támadások, az Alkotmánybíróság ismét dönthet adóügyekben, a testület elnökét a bírók választhatják politikai nyomás nélkül. A Nemzeti Vagyonvisszaszerzési és Vagyonvédelmi Hivatal (NVVH) létrehozását, és az Európai Ügyészséghez csatlakozást is kiemelte, az intézkedéseknek pedig meg is lett a hatása, a tagállami kormányok Tanácsa megszüntette a jogállamisági feltételességi eljárást . Azt is hozzátette, hogy a parlamenti képviselők 12 éves mandátumkorlátozása jogos kérdéseket és aggodalmakat vetett fel, a melegek jogainál is látott hiányosságokat, és azt is megjegyezte, hogy siettek egyes jogszabályokkal, elég idő kell a társadalmi egyeztetéshez. A rendkívüli hatalomhoz jogi biztosítékok kellenek – figyelmeztetett a Tisza Párt kétharmados többségére utalva. „A millió dolláros kérdés természetesen a hetedik cikk” – mondta arról az egyik uniós alapszerződés 7. cikke szerinti eljárásról, amelyet még 2018-ban kezdeményezett az EP. „Egy kis csalódást fogok okozni”: erről nem fognak semmilyen következtetést hozni, nem erre kaptak felhatalmazást, és nem az egész EP álláspontját képviselik, és még írásban is információkat gyűjtenek. Mi a hetedik cikkes eljárás és mi köze a látogatáshoz? A nyolcfős delegáció az EP hivatalos közleménye szerint áttekintette a fejleményeket a 2026. áprilisi választások óta. Ők nyolc különböző frakciót képviselnek. A liberális Sophie Wilmès vezette a küldöttséget. Mellette – egyedüli magyar tagként – László András jött a Fideszből. Többek között a szélsőbaloldaliak és a szélsőjobboldaliak frakciója is delegált egy-egy tagot, a zöldeket Tineke Strik képviselte. Strik az EP-jelentéstevője a „hetedik cikkes” eljárásnak: ezt még 2018-ban kezdeményezte a képviselő-testület, de azóta se előre, se hátra nem haladt a tagállami miniszterek Tanácsában. Az eljárással bizonyos uniós tagságból fakadó jogokat, például a kormány szavazati jogát függeszthetnék fel, ha a tagállami miniszterek megállapítják az uniós alapértékek megsértését, de ennek a lépésnek még a közelében sincsenek. Áprilisban az EU bírósága – a magyar melegellenes törvény miatt – a történetében először hozott olyan ítéletet, amelyben kimondta az uniós alapértékek megsértését , amelyeket az eljárásnak kellene betartatnia. Ahogy arról Strik még májusban beszélt a Telexnek, a mostani októberi kiküldetés lesz „a tökéletes pillanat, hogy az érintettekkel egyeztessünk”: elégedettek-e azzal, ahogyan a dolgok a gyakorlatban működnek. „Talán ez vezethet a jelentésünkhöz egy visszavonási javaslattal.” Az EP november végi plenáris ülésének napirendjében már meg is jelent egy vita a magyar helyzetről azzal, hogy decemberben szavaznak egy állásfoglalásról, erre Wilmès is utalt szerdán. Nem akart belemenni a részletekbe, de jelezte, hogy kezdeményezőként az EP tenné az első lépést. Strik a szerdai sajtótájékoztatón Wilmèshez hasonlóan másnak látta a légkört – nem csak a civilekkel, hanem a hatóságokkal is, amelyek segítőkészek voltak. Szintén látott előrelépéseket, de azt is jelezte, hogy vannak még fejleszteni való területek – például a menekültügynél –, és arányos rendszert szeretnének a következő választásra. A látogatás előtt a volt kormánypártok delegációja és frakciója, a Patrióták Európáért (PfE) kezdeményezte , hogy a küldöttség vizsgálja meg Hankó Balázs, Seszták Miklós és Bús Balázs fogva tartásának körülményeit, de nem látogattak el hozzájuk.
